name: unit-model-compare
notes:
Flip 'unlimited workers' live: off vs on, identical sine load (period 200s) and identical knobs otherwise. Measured (seeds 1-3 alike, same run length): off, the worker pool itself is the admission control per instance -- bounded at ceil(cores*(cpuTimeMs+ioWaitMs)/cpuTimeMs) = ceil(2*(30+120)/30) = 10 worker slots, plus 8 queue slots, so it rejects past capacity. Errors ~3.1%, all of them in the scale-out transient right after load starts; latency stays bounded (max ~264ms, mean ~156ms across the run). On, workers never reject, but the CPU pool (2 cores) still saturates for real: errors drop to 0% -- nothing gets rejected -- but latency balloons: mean ~4.6s (~30x worse), max ~65 SECONDS as queued requests pile up waiting for a core. Instance count is nearly identical either way -- bounded settles at 12 (exactly the needed 12); unlimited settles one higher, at 13 -- because the controller sees almost the same thing in both.

Two things are true at once here, both worth saying out loud:

1. The controller isn't blind, and it isn't the main difference. `cpu` is an honest, time-averaged busy fraction of the real CPU pool (scraped as a cumulative counter, like cgroup cpu usage / Node's eventLoopUtilization). It pins at 100% during the overload in BOTH variants and drives nearly identical scale-out decisions. The one real wrinkle: HPA reads the single latest scrape, not an average -- real HPA doesn't smooth history, it just asks metrics-server for the current number -- so it's more exposed to short-lived spikes. With unlimited workers, cpu stays pinned at 100% noticeably longer (the backlog keeps draining after new capacity arrives), and that longer pinned stretch is enough for one extra HPA sync tick to catch a still-saturated read and add one more instance than the bounded case ever needed.

2. Off, admission control happens once, at the worker pool: a request that can't get a worker (and doesn't fit in the 8-slot queue) is rejected immediately and cleanly, so total in-flight work -- and worst-case latency for anything that IS admitted -- stays bounded. On, there's no admission control left to trip: every request is accepted and simply queues for a core, so the failure mode moves from a fast, honest rejection to a silent, unbounded wait. Zero errors looks like success on a dashboard that only tracks error rate -- it isn't.
